# Scope and conventions

INLAcircular provides probability functions and a model-building interface
for Bayesian circular and joint circular regression with Integrated
Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA). Its core numerical routines are written in
C and exposed through ordinary R functions.

This is the package's user manual and executable R vignette. The repository
HTML and PDF editions are generated from the same source as the installed
vignette, `vignette("INLAcircular-guide", package = "INLAcircular")`.
The function reference, available through `help(package = "INLAcircular")`,
documents individual arguments; this guide explains how to combine them.

Start with Installation and Quick start for a complete example. The later
sections cover distribution functions, priors, structured and joint models,
multivariate effects, troubleshooting, and reproducing the documentation.

The package follows these conventions:

- Angles are measured in radians.
- Location parameters are named `mu`.
- Concentration parameters are named `kappa`, including for
  cardioid and wrapped Cauchy distributions.
- Density functions use `log = TRUE` for log-densities.
- PC-prior distribution and quantile functions use
  `log.p = TRUE` for probabilities on the log scale.
- The d/p/q/r prefix has its usual R meaning: density, distribution function,
  quantile function, and random generation.

The core distribution and PC-prior functions can be used without `INLA`.
Model fitting requires the optional `INLA` package, and LKJ multivariate random
effects also require `graphpcor`.

# Installation

## Requirements

The core package requires R >= 4.1.0 and the R packages listed under
`Depends` and `Imports` in `DESCRIPTION`. R installs these dependencies
automatically. Additional requirements depend on the task:

| Task | Additional requirements |
|:--|:--|
| Distribution functions and PC priors | No INLA installation |
| Model fitting | INLA >= 25.08.21 |
| LKJ multivariate effects | INLA, graphpcor, and INLAtools |
| Build the HTML vignette | knitr, rmarkdown, and Pandoc |
| Rebuild both repository guides | Also pkgload and a LaTeX installation with pdflatex |

Installing from source, including GitHub, compiles the C code in `src/` and
requires the compiler and build tools appropriate for your R installation.
Use Rtools on Windows, the R-supported command-line tools on macOS, or R
development tools and a C compiler on Linux. See the official
[R installation manual](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-admin.html#Installing-packages).
The bundled numerical routines do not require a separate GSL installation.
The optional packages have their own R-version and operating-system
requirements; the core package's minimum R version does not guarantee that
every optional integration is available on that version.

The examples use CPU computation and do not require a GPU. The small
simulations below are intended as installation checks; the full wind and
multivariate applications can need substantially more time and memory.

## Install and load

Install the released version from
[CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/INLAcircular/index.html):

```{r install-cran, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("INLAcircular")
```

The installation above provides the circular distributions and PC-prior
functions without installing INLA. For model fitting, install optional
INLA >= 25.08.21 from the current stable repository separately:

```{r install-inla, eval=FALSE}
install.packages(
  "INLA",
  repos = c(
    getOption("repos"),
    INLA = "https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/stable"
  )
)
```

For the development version from GitHub:

```{r install-package, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github(
  "XiangYEstats/INLAcircular"
)
```

```{r load}
library(INLAcircular)
```

Attaching INLA is optional because `INLAcircular` loads its namespace when a
model-fitting function needs it. If both packages are attached and you want
the compatibility `inla()` function on the search path, load `INLA` first and
then `INLAcircular`.

# Quick start

## Check the numerical functions

This example runs without INLA. It checks the uniform von Mises density and
a PC-prior probability/quantile round trip. Successful checks return `TRUE`.

```{r core-smoke}
isTRUE(all.equal(dvm(0, mu = 0, kappa = 0), 1 / (2 * pi)))
p <- c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)
q <- qpc.vm0(p, lambda = 2)
isTRUE(all.equal(ppc.vm0(q, lambda = 2), p, tolerance = 1e-6))
```

## Create example data

The model examples use this simulated data frame, `dat`. It contains a
circular response `x`, a continuous response `y`, an ordinary covariate `z`,
and hourly node IDs from 1 to 24. The two responses share the simulated
predictor `eta`; a later joint model estimates this association. The seed
makes the input data reproducible.

```{r example-data}
set.seed(2026)
n <- 120
hour <- rep(1:24, length.out = n)
z <- rnorm(n)
eta <- 0.5 + 0.8 * z + 0.25 * sin(2 * pi * hour / 24)
x <- rlavm(n, eta = eta, kappa = 50)
y <- 1 + 0.7 * eta + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)
dat <- data.frame(x = x, y = y, z = z, hour = hour)
stopifnot(all(is.finite(dat$x)), all(abs(dat$x) < pi))
head(dat, 3)
```

Run the model examples in document order: subsequent sections reuse `dat`
and the model settings. Installation commands and explicitly labelled syntax
templates are not executed during rendering. By default, the CRAN vignette
build executes numerical examples and data preparation, while leaving the
optional model fits unevaluated. The repository renderer can execute the fits
with `--run-models`, and the additional LKJ examples with `--run-lkj`; see
Rebuilding and testing below. Code remains visible when a fit is not run.

```{r evaluation-status, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cat(if (run_models) {
  "**This edition:** the ordinary model examples were executed.\n\n"
} else {
  "**This edition:** model fitting code is shown but was not executed.\n\n"
})
cat(if (run_lkj) {
  "The optional LKJ examples were also executed.\n"
} else {
  "The optional LKJ fitting code is shown but was not executed.\n"
})
```

## Fit a circular regression

With INLA installed, specify a LAvM response block and fit it with `inlacc()`.
This initial model estimates a linear effect of `z`; the structured model
later in the guide also accounts for the hourly component.

```{r quick-fit, eval=run_models}
quick_model <- likelihood(x ~ z, family = "lavm")
quick_fit <- inlacc(
  quick_model,
  data = dat,
  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE)
)
columns <- c("mean", "sd", "0.025quant", "0.975quant")
round(quick_fit$summary.fixed[, columns], 3)
round(quick_fit$summary.hyperpar[, columns], 3)
```

The result contains posterior summaries for the intercept and the slope of
`z`, and a natural-scale concentration `kappa`. The simulated slope is
positive. Sampling variability, the omitted hourly effect, and the priors
mean that estimates need not equal the generating parameters. With the
inverse-tangent link, coefficients act on `eta`; they are not changes in
radians per unit of covariate.

## Prepare your own circular data

Supply numeric angles in radians. For LAvM fitting, use a principal interval
strictly inside `(-pi, pi)`, rather than raw degrees or an unwrapped
`[0, 2*pi]` representation. A common preparation is to choose a reference
direction, subtract it, and wrap with `atan2(sin(x), cos(x))`. Record the
reference: model coefficients describe that rotated coordinate system.
Avoid placing observations exactly at the link boundary.

For example, this converts a small degree-valued sample:

```{r angle-input}
degrees <- c(350, 10, 40)
reference <- 0
x <- degrees * pi / 180 - reference
x <- atan2(sin(x), cos(x))
stopifnot(all(is.finite(x)), all(abs(x) < pi))
x
```

Use one row per observation, numeric covariates, and the same row ordering
for all responses in a joint model. Missing responses may be `NA`; the
covariates and latent indices still need valid values for the rows being
modelled. The examples use `x` for circular observations and `y` for an
ordinary response. The transformed variable `z` in the density formula below
is local mathematical notation, distinct from the example covariate.

# Circular distributions

## Quick comparison

The package supplies the full d/p/q/r interface for the von Mises and
link-adjusted von Mises distributions. It supplies compiled densities for the
cardioid and wrapped Cauchy distributions.

```{r density-comparison, fig.cap="Three circular density families with mean direction zero."}
x <- seq(-pi, pi, length.out = 361)
densities <- cbind(
  "von Mises" = dvm(x, mu = 0, kappa = 2),
  "cardioid" = dcardioid(x, mu = 0, kappa = 0.4),
  "wrapped Cauchy" =
    dwrappedcauchy(x, mu = 0, kappa = 0.7)
)

matplot(
  x,
  densities,
  type = "l",
  col = seq_len(ncol(densities)),
  lty = seq_len(ncol(densities)),
  lwd = 2,
  xlab = "Angle (radians)",
  ylab = "Density"
)
legend(
  "topright",
  legend = colnames(densities),
  col = seq_len(ncol(densities)),
  lty = seq_len(ncol(densities)),
  lwd = 2,
  bty = "n"
)
```

## Von Mises

`dvm()`, `pvm()`, `qvm()`, and
`rvm()` evaluate the von Mises distribution with density

\[
f(x\mid\mu,\kappa)
=\frac{\exp\{\kappa\cos(x-\mu)\}}{2\pi I_0(\kappa)}.
\]

`kappa = 0` gives the circular uniform limit. The CDF and quantile
functions use a cached spline grid; `len` controls its resolution.
With `strategy = "circular"`, the CDF origin follows the mean
direction. The alternative `strategy = "linear"` retains a fixed
linear representation.

```{r von-mises-api}
set.seed(1)
rvm(5, mu = 0, kappa = 3)
pvm(pi / 2, mu = 0, kappa = 2)
qvm(0.95, mu = 0, kappa = 2)
```

## Link-adjusted von Mises

`dlavm()`, `plavm()`, `qlavm()`, and
`rlavm()` use a linear predictor `eta` and concentration
`kappa`. The current direct distribution interface uses the
inverse-tangent transformation

\[
z=2\arctan\{\tan(x/2)-\eta\}.
\]

`lavm.link("tan")` returns the corresponding transformation and
inverse functions. The `link_obj` argument in the p/q/r functions
is reserved for interface compatibility; the current compiled implementation
uses the inverse-tangent link.

```{r lavm-api}
set.seed(2)
rlavm(5, eta = 1.5, kappa = 3)
dlavm(c(-1, 0, 1), eta = 1.5, kappa = 3)
plavm(pi / 2, eta = 1.5, kappa = 3)
qlavm(0.5, eta = 1.5, kappa = 3)
```

## Cardioid and wrapped Cauchy densities

The cardioid density is

\[
f_{\mathrm{card}}(x\mid\mu,\kappa)
=\frac{1+2\kappa\cos(x-\mu)}{2\pi},
\qquad 0\leq\kappa\leq\frac12.
\]

Use `dcardioid()`, or its short alias `dcard()`.

The wrapped Cauchy density is

\[
f_{\mathrm{wc}}(x\mid\mu,\kappa)
=\frac{1-\kappa^2}
 {2\pi\{1+\kappa^2-2\kappa\cos(x-\mu)\}},
\qquad 0\leq\kappa<1.
\]

Use `dwrappedcauchy()`, or its short alias `dwc()`.
The endpoint `kappa = 1` is a point-mass limit: the compiled
density reports `Inf` at the mean direction and zero elsewhere.
Finite-parameter likelihoods should use `kappa < 1`.

Both functions recycle `x`, `mu`, and
`kappa` to a common length.

```{r other-densities}
x <- c(-pi / 2, 0, pi / 2)
dcardioid(x, mu = 0, kappa = c(0, 0.25, 0.5))
dwrappedcauchy(x, mu = 0, kappa = 0.7, log = TRUE)
```

# Penalized-complexity priors

A PC prior assigns an exponential distribution with rate
`lambda` to a distance from a simpler base model. Larger
`lambda` puts more prior mass near the base. All five prior
families expose matching density, CDF, quantile, and random-generation
functions.

| Help topic | Base model | Support for kappa | Special behavior |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| pc.vm0 | von Mises uniform limit, kappa = 0 | [0, Inf) | Continuous |
| pc.vminf | von Mises point-mass limit | [0, Inf) | Atom exp(-lambda) at zero |
| pc.card0 | cardioid uniform model, kappa = 0 | [0, 1/2] | Normalized truncated exponential distance |
| pc.card | cardioid base, kappa = 1/2 | [0, 1/2] | Atom at zero; integrable singularity at 1/2 |
| pc.wc | wrapped Cauchy uniform model, kappa = 0 | [0, 1) | Continuous; open upper endpoint |

For a monotone distance \(d(\kappa)\), an untruncated continuous PC prior has
density

\[
\pi(\kappa)=\lambda\exp\{-\lambda d(\kappa)\}
              \left|d'(\kappa)\right|.
\]

When the attainable distance range is bounded, the remaining exponential
tail must be handled explicitly. `pc.card0` truncates and normalizes
the exponential distance law; `pc.vminf` and `pc.card`
collapse the remaining tail to a boundary atom. The density functions below
return densities with respect to Lebesgue measure. A boundary atom is therefore
represented by the CDF and RNG, not added to the value returned by a density
function.

## Von Mises prior with uniform base: pc.vm0

Write

\[
A(\kappa)=\frac{I_1(\kappa)}{I_0(\kappa)},\qquad
A'(\kappa)=1-A(\kappa)^2-\frac{A(\kappa)}{\kappa},
\]

where the continuous limit is \(A'(0)=1/2\). The distance from the circular
uniform model is

\[
d_0(\kappa)=
\sqrt{\kappa A(\kappa)-\log I_0(\kappa)}.
\]

For \(\kappa>0\), the density and CDF are

\[
\boxed{
\pi_0(\kappa)=
\lambda e^{-\lambda d_0(\kappa)}
\frac{\kappa A'(\kappa)}{2d_0(\kappa)}
},\qquad
F_0(\kappa)=1-e^{-\lambda d_0(\kappa)}.
\]

The density has the finite endpoint limit
\(\pi_0(0)=\lambda/2\). This is a continuous distribution with no atom at
zero. Use `dpc.vm0()`, `ppc.vm0()`,
`qpc.vm0()`, and `rpc.vm0()`.

```{r pc-vm}
probability <- c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)
q0 <- qpc.vm0(probability, lambda = 2)
cbind(
  probability = probability,
  quantile = q0,
  recovered = ppc.vm0(q0, lambda = 2)
)

dpc.vm0(c(0, 0.5, 2), lambda = 2)
```

## Von Mises prior with point-mass base: pc.vminf

The distance from the point-mass limit \(\kappa\rightarrow\infty\) is

\[
d_\infty(\kappa)=\sqrt{1-A(\kappa)}.
\]

The continuous density for \(\kappa>0\) and the full CDF are

\[
\boxed{
\pi_\infty^{\mathrm{cont}}(\kappa)=
\lambda e^{-\lambda d_\infty(\kappa)}
\frac{A'(\kappa)}{2d_\infty(\kappa)}
},\qquad
F_\infty(\kappa)=e^{-\lambda d_\infty(\kappa)}.
\]

Because \(d_\infty(0)=1\), the full law has boundary mass
\(\Pr(\kappa=0)=e^{-\lambda}\). `dpc.vminf()` returns only the
continuous component, whose right-hand endpoint limit is
\(\lambda e^{-\lambda}/4\). `ppc.vminf()`,
`qpc.vminf()`, and `rpc.vminf()` include the atom.

```{r pc-vminf}
lambda <- 2
atom_vm <- exp(-lambda)
c(computed = ppc.vminf(0, lambda), expected = atom_vm)
dpc.vminf(c(0, 0.5, 2), lambda)
qpc.vminf(c(atom_vm / 2, (1 + atom_vm) / 2), lambda)
```

## Cardioid prior with uniform base: pc.card0

Let

\[
s(\kappa)=\sqrt{1-4\kappa^2},\qquad
d_0(\kappa)=
\sqrt{1-s(\kappa)+\log\{(1+s(\kappa))/2\}}.
\]

The distance is bounded above by
\(D_0=\sqrt{1-\log 2}\). Therefore pc.card0 uses the normalized,
truncated exponential density

\[
\boxed{
\pi_0(\kappa)=
\frac{\lambda e^{-\lambda d_0(\kappa)}}
     {1-e^{-\lambda D_0}}
\frac{2\kappa}{\{1+s(\kappa)\}d_0(\kappa)}
}.
\]

Its CDF is

\[
F_0(\kappa)=
\frac{1-\exp\{-\lambda d_0(\kappa)\}}
 {1-\exp(-\lambda D_0)}.
\]

Use `dpc.card0()`, `ppc.card0()`,
`qpc.card0()`, and `rpc.card0()`.
The density at zero is evaluated by continuity and equals
\(\lambda/\{1-e^{-\lambda D_0}\}\). At \(\kappa=1/2\), it equals
\(\lambda e^{-\lambda D_0}/[D_0\{1-e^{-\lambda D_0}\}]\).

```{r pc-card0}
probability <- c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)
quantile <- qpc.card0(probability, lambda = 2)
cbind(
  probability = probability,
  quantile = quantile,
  recovered = ppc.card0(quantile, lambda = 2)
)
dpc.card0(c(0, 0.25, 0.5), lambda = 2)
```

## Cardioid prior with base kappa = 1/2: pc.card

The distance to the concentrated cardioid base is

\[
d_{1/2}(\kappa)=
\sqrt{1-2\kappa-s(\kappa)+\log\{1+s(\kappa)\}}.
\]

It decreases from \(\sqrt{\log 2}\) at zero to zero at the base. Its
continuous density is

\[
\boxed{
\pi_{1/2}^{\mathrm{cont}}(\kappa)=
\lambda e^{-\lambda d_{1/2}(\kappa)}
\frac{1+s(\kappa)-2\kappa}
     {\{1+s(\kappa)\}d_{1/2}(\kappa)}
}.
\]

The full CDF is

\[
F_{1/2}(\kappa)=\exp\{-\lambda d_{1/2}(\kappa)\}.
\]

Consequently, the distribution has boundary mass
\(\exp\{-\lambda\sqrt{\log 2}\}\) at `kappa = 0`.
`dpc.card()` returns the continuous density component.
`ppc.card()`, `qpc.card()`, and
`rpc.card()` include the atom. The continuous density tends to
`Inf` at `kappa = 0.5`, but the singularity is
integrable. At zero, its continuous component is
\(\lambda e^{-\lambda\sqrt{\log 2}}/\sqrt{\log 2}\); this value is distinct
from the atom probability.

```{r pc-card}
lambda <- 2
atom_card <- exp(-lambda * sqrt(log(2)))
c(computed = ppc.card(0, lambda), expected = atom_card)
qpc.card(c(atom_card / 2, (1 + atom_card) / 2), lambda)
dpc.card(c(0, 0.25, 0.49), lambda)
```

## Wrapped Cauchy prior: pc.wc

For the wrapped Cauchy family,

\[
d_{\mathrm{wc}}(\kappa)=\sqrt{-\log(1-\kappa^2)}
\]

maps [0, 1) to the full nonnegative distance axis. Its density is

\[
\boxed{
\pi_{\mathrm{wc}}(\kappa)=
\lambda e^{-\lambda d_{\mathrm{wc}}(\kappa)}
\frac{\kappa}{(1-\kappa^2)d_{\mathrm{wc}}(\kappa)}
}.
\]

The CDF is

\[
F_{\mathrm{wc}}(\kappa)
=1-\exp\{-\lambda d_{\mathrm{wc}}(\kappa)\}.
\]

Use `dpc.wc()`, `ppc.wc()`,
`qpc.wc()`, and `rpc.wc()`. The density limit at zero
is `lambda`; the density diverges as `kappa`
approaches one. Interior-probability quantiles (`0 < p < 1`) and RNG output
remain strictly below one. There is no atom at one; the value
`dpc.wc(1, lambda)` is the limiting density convention.

```{r pc-wc}
q_wc <- qpc.wc(c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), lambda = 2)
cbind(quantile = q_wc, recovered = ppc.wc(q_wc, lambda = 2))

set.seed(3)
rpc.wc(5, lambda = 2)
dpc.wc(c(0, 0.5, 0.9), lambda = 2)
```

## Density, probability, and vectorization rules

Every family follows the same call pattern:

```r
dpc.NAME(kappa, lambda, log = FALSE)
ppc.NAME(q, lambda, log.p = FALSE)
qpc.NAME(p, lambda, log.p = FALSE)
rpc.NAME(n, lambda)
```

The PC-prior functions recycle concentrations or probabilities against
`lambda`. The rate must always contain positive, finite values.
With `log.p = TRUE`, CDFs return log-probabilities and quantiles
accept log-probabilities. The density flag is `log`, and both flags
must be one non-missing logical value. There is no `lower.tail`
argument; all probabilities are lower-tail.

Values and `lambda` recycle to their common maximum length, with a
warning for non-multiple lengths. For random generation, a vector
`n` requests `length(n)` draws; otherwise its scalar value
is converted to an integer. The generators use R's RNG stream. Apart from the
documented limiting-endpoint conventions, densities are zero outside their
mathematical support, while invalid probabilities produce `NaN`.

Names such as `pc.card0` are help topics and prior labels, not
callable R functions. Use the corresponding d/p/q/r functions.

```{r pc-log-vector}
dpc.card0(c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3), lambda = c(1, 2, 3), log = TRUE)
qpc.wc(log(c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)), lambda = 2, log.p = TRUE)
```

# LAvM likelihood

Use `family = "lavm"` with `inla()` or
`inlacc()` from INLAcircular. The LAvM likelihood is implemented
using INLA's compiled `cloglike` interface. The package handles response
preparation automatically.

The following settings can be supplied as `control.family` in
`inla()` or as `family.setting` in
`likelihood()`:

```{r lavm-settings}
lavm_setting <- list(
  link = "inverse.tangent",
  hyper = list(
    kappa = list(
      initial = log(50),
      prior = "pc.vminf",
      param = c(0.5, 0.5),
      fixed = FALSE
    )
  )
)
```

## LAvM likelihood controls

The LAvM settings accept the following controls:

- `link` is `"inverse.tangent"` (the default),
  `"scaled.logit"`, or `"scaled.probit"`.
- `hyper$kappa$initial` is one finite initial value for
  \(\theta=\log(\kappa)\). The default is 6; it is not a natural-scale
  concentration.
- `hyper$kappa$prior` is `"pc.vminf"` (the default) or
  `"pc.vm0"`.
- `hyper$kappa$param = c(u, alpha)` contains two values strictly
  between zero and one. Here \(u\) is a threshold for the mean resultant
  length \(A(\kappa)=I_1(\kappa)/I_0(\kappa)\), and the calibration is
  \(\Pr\{A(\kappa)>u\}=\alpha\).
- `hyper$kappa$fixed = TRUE` fixes
  \(\log(\kappa)\) at `initial`; the default is
  `FALSE`.

If \(\kappa_u\) solves \(A(\kappa_u)=u\), `pc.vm0` uses

\[
\lambda=-\frac{\log(\alpha)}{d_0(\kappa_u)},
\]

whereas `pc.vminf` uses

\[
\lambda=-\frac{\log(1-\alpha)}{\sqrt{1-u}}.
\]

This `c(u, alpha)` interface differs from the standalone d/p/q/r
functions, which take `lambda` directly.

For `pc.vminf`, this calibration comes from the full PC law,
including its atom at `kappa = 0`. A fitted INLA hyperparameter is
finite \(\theta=\log(\kappa)\), so model fitting uses only the continuous
component transformed to the \(\theta\) scale, including its Jacobian. It has
no separate discrete state at \(\theta=-\infty\). Treat
`c(u, alpha)` as the rate calibration for the fitted continuous
prior, not as a claim that the fitted hyperparameter retains the boundary
atom.

## Fitting with `inla()`

A single LAvM model can be fitted with `inla()` without using
`inlacc()`. Loading INLAcircular makes its `inla()`
function available. If you also attach INLA, load it first and INLAcircular
second. The example below uses `x` for the circular response and
`z` for an ordinary covariate, both taken from the simulated `dat`.

```{r convenient-inla, eval=run_models}
library(INLAcircular)

fit_short <- inla(
  x ~ z,
  family = "lavm",
  data = dat,
  control.family = lavm_setting
)

columns <- c("mean", "sd", "0.025quant", "0.975quant")
round(fit_short$summary.fixed[, columns], 3)
round(fit_short$summary.hyperpar[, columns], 3)
```

The package reports the concentration on the natural `kappa`
scale. Use `INLAcircular::inla()` if you need to select this
function explicitly. Calls with other likelihood families are forwarded to
INLA.

# Building model specifications

`inlacc()` uses a formula-building layer to assemble one or more
likelihood blocks into a stacked INLA model. Create one response block with

```r
likelihood(formula, family, family.setting = NULL)
```

Its arguments are:

- `formula`: a two-sided formula for one response. The left side
  should be a single column name in `data`.
- `family`: one INLA likelihood name. Use `"lavm"` for
  the package's link-adjusted von Mises likelihood; other names are passed to
  INLA.
- `family.setting`: the `control.family` list for this
  block. For LAvM it has the structure documented in the preceding section.

A single likelihood object can be passed directly to `inlacc()`.
A joint model is a list. Likelihood order determines response-block order and,
where relevant, multivariate component order.

```{r model-specification}
x_model <- likelihood(
  x ~
    intercept(name = "alpha0", mean = 0, sd = 2) +
    covariate(z, name = "alpha_z", mean = 0, sd = 1) +
    f(
      hour_effect,
      model = "rw1",
      cyclic = TRUE,
      constr = TRUE,
      scale.model = TRUE,
      hyper = list(
        prec = list(
          prior = "pc.prec",
          param = c(1, 0.01)
        )
      )
    ),
  family = "lavm",
  family.setting = lavm_setting
)
```

## Formula terms and their interpretation

The right side may contain ordinary numeric fixed-effect expressions and the
following markers:

| Term | Meaning inside `inlacc()` |
|:--|:--|
| `1` | Automatic block-specific intercept named `Intercept_<response>` |
| `0` or `-1` | Remove the automatic intercept |
| `intercept(...)` | Named intercept with an optional Gaussian prior |
| ordinary term such as `z` or `log(z)` | Block-specific fixed effect evaluated in `data` |
| `covariate(...)` | Fixed effect or automatically/explicitly copied response predictor |
| `f(...)` | Standard INLA latent-effect term, passed into the assembled formula |

Use numeric columns and expressions for ordinary terms. The assembler does
not reproduce every `model.matrix()` feature for factors, offsets,
or special response expressions. Use unique custom coefficient names across
likelihoods unless a shared fixed coefficient is intentional.

### `intercept()`

```r
intercept(name = NULL, mean = NULL, sd = NULL)
```

- `name` changes the coefficient label; its default is
  `Intercept_<response>`.
- `mean` and `sd` set the Gaussian prior. A missing value
  inherits the corresponding global fixed-effect setting.
- A formula `0` or `-1` removes the automatic intercept,
  while an explicit `intercept()` adds the custom one.

This is a formula marker. It returns `NULL` when called by itself
because `inlacc()` interprets its unevaluated call.

### `covariate()`

```r
covariate(
  var,
  name = NULL,
  mean = NULL,
  sd = NULL,
  initial = NULL,
  fixed = FALSE,
  predictor = NULL
)
```

- `var` is an unquoted variable or expression evaluated in
  `data`. It is an argument, not a separate function named
  `var()`.
- `name` supplies a stable coefficient and display name.
- `mean` and `sd` independently override the Gaussian
  prior for an ordinary fixed effect.
- `predictor = NULL`, the default, copies the latent predictor when
  `var` is an untransformed response in another likelihood block;
  otherwise it creates an ordinary observed fixed effect.
- `predictor = TRUE` explicitly requests copying. It is an error if
  `var` is not an untransformed response from another block.
- `predictor = FALSE` always creates an ordinary fixed effect from
  the observed values, including when `var` is another response.
- `initial` and `fixed` control the INLA copy-scaling
  coefficient. They apply to copied predictors and are not used for ordinary
  fixed effects.

For a copied predictor, provide both `mean` and `sd` to
customize its scaling prior. If either is absent, the current implementation
uses its default \(N(0,31.62^2)\) scaling prior. Any response used directly as
a bare term on another block's right side is also copied automatically. To use
that response's observed values instead, write
`covariate(response, predictor = FALSE)`. A transformed expression
such as `log(response)` is an ordinary observed fixed effect under
`predictor = NULL` or `FALSE`; requesting
`predictor = TRUE` for a transformed expression is an error because
this interface can copy only a named source predictor.

### `f()` and standard INLA options

INLAcircular does not export a separate `f()`. Write a bare
`f(...)` in an `inlacc()` formula. Its syntax is the
R-INLA latent-effect syntax, including `model`, `hyper`,
`constr`, `scale.model`, `cyclic`,
`group`, `control.group`, `replicate`,
`values`, and `copy`. Use
`INLA::inla.doc()` for details of the selected latent model.

The term is preserved in the assembled INLA formula. INLAcircular additionally
does the following:

- supplies an index column from `data` or `index()`;
- creates `1:nrow(data)` when an index is otherwise absent;
- injects or replaces `values` for the matching first index when a
  complete `process.id` is given;
- records common model and hyperprior information for summaries; and
- rewrites the special `model = "iidkd_LKJ"` form described later.

Because the preprocessor recognizes the call name literally, use
`f(...)`, not `INLA::f(...)`, in these formulas.

## Mapping observations with `index()`

```r
index(var, data.id, process.id = NULL)
```

Here `data.id` and `process.id` are arguments of
`index()`, not separate functions.

- `var` is a character string matching the first argument of an
  `f()` term.
- `data.id` maps each observation row to a latent-process node and
  should normally have `nrow(data)` entries.
- `process.id` optionally gives the complete ordered node set. When
  supplied, it becomes the INLA `values` argument for an
  `f()` term whose first argument matches `var`, replacing
  any existing `values` argument. When it is `NULL`, INLA
  infers represented values from the observation index. A mapping can supply
  `data.id` for a first, group, or replicate variable, but
  `process.id` applies only to a matching first index.

```{r latent-index}
hour_index <- index(
  var = "hour_effect",
  data.id = c(1, 2, 2, 4),
  process.id = 1:24
)

hour_index
```

Pass one object directly or several in a list. This example supplies the
hourly mapping for `x_model`, using node IDs from 1 to 24:

```{r multiple-indices}
latent_indices <- list(
  index("hour_effect", data.id = dat$hour, process.id = 1:24)
)
```

Add one `index()` object for each additional latent process. Each mapping
must match an index actually used in the model.

If a mapped name is not used by any `f()` first, group, or
replicate argument, it is ignored with a warning. For an ordinary shared
effect, `index(var, data.id = "likelihood")` sets its index to the
likelihood-block number. A later section documents the different special LKJ
form `process.id = "likelihood"`.

# Fitting with `inlacc()`

The complete call is

```r
inlacc(
  model,
  data,
  latent.index = NULL,
  LKJ.eta = 5,
  control.family = NULL,
  control.fixed = NULL,
  control.inla = list(cmin = 0, compute.initial.values = TRUE),
  metrics = FALSE,
  verbose = FALSE,
  ...
)
```

## Arguments and defaults

- `model` is one `likelihood()` object or a non-empty
  list of them.
- `data` is a data frame containing every simple response column,
  fixed-effect variable, and ordinary latent index. All likelihood blocks use
  the same number and ordering of observation rows; missing responses are
  represented with `NA` and handled by INLA.
- `latent.index` is one `index()` object or a list of
  them.
- `LKJ.eta` is one positive finite LKJ shape shared by every
  `iidkd_LKJ` group. It defaults to 5 and is irrelevant when no
  such group is present.
- `control.family` optionally overrides block-level
  `family.setting`. Supply one nested control list per likelihood,
  even for a single block. When no override exists for a block, that block's
  `family.setting` is used.
- `control.fixed` is an INLA fixed-effect control list. The package
  defaults are mean 0 and precision 0.001, equivalent to SD about 31.62.
  Its `mean` and `prec` may be scalars or INLA named lists
  with a `default` entry; existing named entries are preserved.
  Priors specified in `intercept()` or `covariate()`
  override the matching coefficients.
- `control.inla` is passed to `INLA::inla()`. By default,
  `cmin` is 0 and `compute.initial.values` is `TRUE`.
  Supplying another list replaces
  that whole default, so include either setting explicitly when it remains
  required.
- `metrics = TRUE` requests CPO, DIC, WAIC, and INLA configuration
  output. The default is `FALSE`.
- `verbose` is passed directly to `INLA::inla()`.
- `...` accepts further INLA arguments. Common examples are
  `control.predictor`, `control.compute`,
  `control.mode`, and `num.threads`. A supplied `control.compute` is
  merged field by field with the values implied by `metrics`.

Do not pass `formula` or `family` through
`...`: those names would replace the internally assembled values.
Use the formal `control.family` and `control.fixed`
arguments only for their documented controls; the stacked formula and data are
owned by `inlacc()`.

## Single-likelihood fit

```{r inlacc-fit, eval=run_models}
fit <- inlacc(
  model = x_model,
  data = dat,
  latent.index = index(
    "hour_effect",
    data.id = dat$hour,
    process.id = 1:24
  ),
  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
  metrics = TRUE
)
```

## Joint likelihoods and copied predictors

This example fits both simulated responses in `dat`. The first block is
`x_model`, including its hourly effect. The second uses the first block's
latent predictor through an INLA copy term.
Because `x` is the response of another likelihood block,
`covariate(x)` selects this behavior automatically.

```{r joint-inlacc, eval=run_models}
joint_model <- list(
  x_model,
  likelihood(
    y ~
      intercept(name = "beta0", mean = 0, sd = 5) +
      covariate(
        x,
        name = "beta_x",
        mean = 0,
        sd = 1,
        initial = 0,
        fixed = FALSE
      ),
    family = "gaussian",
    family.setting = list(
      hyper = list(
        prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01))
      )
    )
  )
)

joint_fit <- inlacc(
  model = joint_model,
  data = dat,
  latent.index = latent_indices,
  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
  metrics = TRUE
)
joint_summary <- summary(joint_fit)
round(joint_summary$fixed_par[, c("mean", "SD", "2.5%", "97.5%")], 3)
round(joint_summary$random_par[
  "beta_x", c("mean", "SD", "2.5%", "97.5%"), drop = FALSE
], 3)
```

The Gaussian block contains the copied predictor without an additional
effect of `z`: duplicating the same linear information can make the copy
coefficient difficult to identify. Here `beta_x` describes the association
with the circular block's latent `eta`, not with its observed angle in radians.
Copy coefficients are INLA hyperparameters, so the package summary places
`beta_x` in `random_par` rather than `fixed_par`.

Writing `predictor = TRUE` in that term is equivalent but makes the
copy request explicit. To regress on the observed angles instead of their
latent predictor, use
`covariate(x, predictor = FALSE)`.

Set `control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE)` when fitted linear
predictors are needed. The custom summary warns when predictor computation is
particularly relevant, including models with copied covariates.

## Returned object

The result inherits from both `inlacc` and INLA result classes, so
ordinary INLA components remain available. The package also records:

- the assembled formula, stacked data, effective families, and family
  controls in `inlacc_meta`;
- fixed-effect, hyperparameter, prior, and latent-process mappings used by
  `summary.inlacc()`;
- the names of copied predictors; and
- `lkj_modes` and `inlacc_meta$LKJ`, both always lists and
  empty when no LKJ effect is present.

LAvM concentration marginals are normally transformed from
\(\log(\kappa)\) to \(\kappa\) and renamed in the fitted object. Raw INLA
fields such as `summary.fixed`, `summary.hyperpar`,
`marginals.fixed`, `marginals.hyperpar`,
`summary.fitted.values`, and `cpu.used` remain available.

# Modelling multivariate effects with `graphpcor`

INLAcircular integrates one specific graphpcor model: a dense
LKJ-correlated IID vector shared across likelihood blocks. It does not expose
graphpcor's general graph-structured or tree-structured model interfaces.

Install the optional dependencies before using this feature:

```{r graphpcor-install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages(c("graphpcor", "INLAtools"))
```

The feature inherits graphpcor's own R-version and dependency requirements.
Both packages are checked at run time.

Some INLAtools versions first look for a separate graphpcor shared library
and warn if it is absent. An INLA executable with a built-in LKJ model can
still complete the fit. Use `verbose = TRUE` to confirm which model was
selected; otherwise a compatible compiled graphpcor library is needed.
A path warning alone is not evidence of a successful or failed fit. The
examples below proceed to inspect the fitted covariance parameters.

## Declaring an LKJ-correlated effect

Use the exact special syntax

```r
f(
  i,
  model = "iidkd_LKJ",
  pc.prior.u = 1,
  pc.prior.alpha = 0.5
)
```

in at least two likelihood blocks. Terms with the same bare first argument
(`i` above) form one multivariate process. Component order follows
the likelihood objects supplied to `inlacc()`.

- A process may occur at most once in each likelihood.
- Its dimension is the number of likelihoods containing the term and must be
  at least two.
- The same index name cannot also be used by another `f()` model.
- `LKJ.eta` is supplied once to `inlacc()`, not as
  `eta` inside `f()`.
- `prior.param` is not supported for this special term.

The per-component scale prior is passed to graphpcor as
`sigma.prior.reference = pc.prior.u` and
`sigma.prior.probability = pc.prior.alpha`. The defaults are 1 and
0.5. The reference must be positive; the probability may be in [0, 1] or
`NA`. The PC-scale calibration used by the implementation is
\(\Pr(\sigma>u)=\alpha\), equivalently
\(\lambda=-\log(\alpha)/u\). Values `0`, `1`, and
`NA` fix that component's standard deviation at `u`
rather than estimating a scale parameter.

This separate simulation creates two responses with correlated latent
intercepts, using one replicate per row. It does not overwrite `dat`.

```{r graphpcor-data}
set.seed(2027)
n_lkj <- 60
b <- matrix(rnorm(2 * n_lkj), ncol = 2) %*%
  chol(matrix(c(0.25, 0.15, 0.15, 0.36), nrow = 2))
dat_lkj <- data.frame(
  x = rlavm(n_lkj, eta = b[, 1], kappa = 50),
  y = b[, 2] + rnorm(n_lkj, sd = 0.2)
)
```

```{r graphpcor-model, eval=run_lkj}
multivariate_model <- list(
  likelihood(
    x ~ intercept(name = "alpha0") +
      f(
        i,
        model = "iidkd_LKJ",
        pc.prior.u = 1,
        pc.prior.alpha = 0.5
      ),
    family = "lavm",
    family.setting = lavm_setting
  ),
  likelihood(
    y ~ intercept(name = "beta0") +
      f(
        i,
        model = "iidkd_LKJ",
        pc.prior.u = 2,
        pc.prior.alpha = 0.5
      ),
    family = "gaussian"
  )
)

fit_lkj <- inlacc(
  multivariate_model,
  data = dat_lkj,
  LKJ.eta = 5,
  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE)
)
```

`LKJcc()` performs the preprocessing internally: it collects the
terms, constructs graphpcor's cgeneric model, rewrites the formulas, and
creates component and replicate indices. Most users should not call it
directly. Its return value contains the rewritten formulas, generated models,
block data, process metadata, and unconsumed ordinary index mappings.

## Replicate indices

By default, observations receive replicate IDs
`seq_len(nrow(data))`; no `i` column is required. To use
explicit replicate IDs, supply the special mapping

```{r graphpcor-index, eval=run_lkj}
replicate_id <- seq_len(nrow(dat_lkj))
lkj_index <- index(
  var = "i",
  data.id = replicate_id,
  process.id = "likelihood"
)

fit_lkj <- inlacc(
  multivariate_model,
  data = dat_lkj,
  latent.index = lkj_index,
  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
  LKJ.eta = 5
)
```

In this special form, `data.id` must contain one positive integer
per observation and becomes the INLA replicate index. The component index is
generated from likelihood order. An explicit
`replicate = some_name` must use a bare variable name. It may be
written in one or more special `f()` terms, but every explicit name
within a group must agree. That name controls the generated replicate column;
its values still come from this mapping or the default row sequence.

## Recovering covariance information

`fit_lkj$lkj_modes[["i"]]` stores internal posterior-mode values,
not a full posterior correlation summary. When every scale is free
(`0 < pc.prior.alpha < 1`), the first \(p\) entries for a
\(p\)-dimensional group are log standard deviations and the remaining
\(p(p-1)/2\) entries parameterize the correlation matrix. The example above
has this all-free form.

```{r graphpcor-reconstruct, eval=run_lkj}
p <- 2L
theta_i <- fit_lkj$lkj_modes[["i"]]

sd_mode <- exp(theta_i[seq_len(p)])
correlation_mode <- graphpcor::basecor(
  theta_i[-seq_len(p)],
  p = p
)$base

sd_mode
correlation_mode
```

For a mixture of free and fixed scales, reconstruct the complete SD vector
before extracting the correlation parameters. The following code also works
for the all-free example above:

```{r graphpcor-reconstruct-fixed, eval=run_lkj}
process_i <- fit_lkj$inlacc_meta$LKJ[["i"]]
u <- process_i$pc.prior.u
alpha <- process_i$pc.prior.alpha
fixed_scale <- is.na(alpha) | alpha <= 0 | alpha >= 1
n_free <- sum(!fixed_scale)

theta_i <- fit_lkj$lkj_modes[["i"]]
log_sd_mode <- log(u)
log_sd_mode[!fixed_scale] <- theta_i[seq_len(n_free)]

n_cor <- p * (p - 1L) / 2L
cor_index <- n_free + seq_len(n_cor)
correlation_mode <- graphpcor::basecor(
  theta_i[cor_index],
  p = p
)$base

sd_mode <- exp(log_sd_mode)
```

For multiple LKJ groups, use the corresponding first-argument name as the
list key. Component order is always the likelihood order used to build the
group. These are point estimates at the internal posterior mode; use INLA's
marginal or sampling tools when full uncertainty summaries are required.

# Results and summaries

`summary()` dispatches to `summary.inlacc()` for fitted
models:

```r
summary(object, decimal = 3, ...)
```

It returns an `inlacc_summary` object with the following components:

- `fixed_par`: fixed-effect posterior summaries and displayed
  Gaussian priors;
- `likelihood_par`: transformed likelihood parameters, including
  natural-scale LAvM concentration and Gaussian standard deviations;
- `random_par`: latent-process hyperparameters and their prior
  labels;
- `time.summary`: setup, computation, post-processing, and total
  times;
- `metrics`: available marginal likelihood, DIC, and WAIC summaries;
  and
- `needs_pred_warning`: whether the fitted model would benefit from
  `control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE)`.

The `decimal` value controls printing, not stored posterior
precision. `print.inlacc_summary(x, decimal = NULL, metrics = TRUE)`
can override the number of displayed decimal places and suppress the metrics
section. Timing components use
`print.inlacc_time(x)`. These methods are normally called through
`summary()` and `print()` rather than directly.

```{r summaries, eval=run_models}
fit_summary <- summary(fit, decimal = 3)
round(fit_summary$fixed_par[, c("mean", "SD", "2.5%", "97.5%")], 3)
```

The selected columns above give a compact table. For the full console
printout, including priors and timing, use:

```{r print-summary, eval=FALSE}
print(fit_summary, metrics = TRUE)
```

Because an `inlacc` result remains an INLA result, the original
posterior summaries, marginals, fitted values, predictor values, model
criteria, and timing fields remain accessible with standard INLA component
names. CPO values remain on the raw fit even though the custom printed summary
does not create a separate CPO table.

## Extract predictors on the right scale

For a single response, the first `nrow(dat)` predictor rows correspond to
the observations. In a joint fit, requested response blocks are stacked in
likelihood order. Copied predictors can introduce additional auxiliary rows
after those response blocks, so do not assume every returned row is a new
observation.

```{r predictor-output, eval=run_models}
n <- nrow(dat)
eta_x <- joint_fit$summary.linear.predictor[seq_len(n), ]
eta_y <- joint_fit$summary.linear.predictor[n + seq_len(n), ]
head(eta_x[, c("mean", "sd", "0.025quant", "0.975quant")], 3)
head(eta_y[, c("mean", "sd")], 3)
```

For the inverse-tangent LAvM link, `2 * atan(eta)` is the conditional
location/median parameter. Transforming posterior quantiles of `eta`
gives quantiles of this parameter. It is not the same calculation as a
posterior predictive circular mean or a prediction interval for a new angle.

```{r location-output, eval=run_models}
location <- 2 * atan(
  as.matrix(eta_x[, c("0.025quant", "0.5quant", "0.975quant")])
)
head(location, 3)
```

When data were rotated before fitting, add the recorded reference direction
and wrap again to report locations in the original coordinates. Inspect
`summary.linear.predictor` for `eta`; do not assume
`summary.fitted.values` contains circular means.

The fitted LAvM interface does not currently provide a CDF for INLA's PIT
diagnostics. Requesting `metrics = TRUE` does not make LAvM PIT available.
Check available CPO values and their failure indicators, and interpret DIC
or WAIC comparisons only for models fitted to the same responses and data.

# Utilities and included data

## Modified Bessel function

`bessel_i(x, nu, expon.scaled = FALSE)` evaluates the modified
Bessel function of the first kind using C routines adapted from GSL. R is
only the interface. The order `nu` must be finite and nonnegative;
fractional orders are supported for nonnegative `x`. Negative
`x` is supported for integer orders, with the usual parity rule;
otherwise it produces `NaN` and a warning. Set
`expon.scaled = TRUE` to return \(I_\nu(x)\exp(-|x|)\), which
avoids overflow for large x.
Very large orders can reduce the accuracy of unscaled values near the
transition between exponential growth and decay; such inputs produce an
accuracy warning when the estimated loss is significant.

```{r bessel}
bessel_i(c(0, 1, 5), nu = 0)
bessel_i(1, nu = 0.5)
bessel_i(1000, nu = 0, expon.scaled = TRUE)
```

## New York wind data

`wind_newyork` contains 8,759 hourly climate-normal records for JFK
International Airport (station USW00094789), supplied with the New York wind
application. Its UTC calendar uses 2010 as a reference year; these are not
8,759 observed weather measurements taken in 2010. The first record is
January 1 at 01:00, so the reference calendar lacks January 1 at 00:00.

The principal fields are `HLY.WIND.VCTDIR` (circular direction in radians),
`HLY.WIND.VCTSPD` (wind speed), `HLY.TEMP.NORMAL` (temperature), and
`hour` (0 through 23). `DATE`, `datetime`, `month`, and `day` complete the
eight columns. See `?wind_newyork` for the stored schema. The included
metadata does not specify the original speed/temperature units or the
climate-normal baseline period; establish those from the upstream dataset
before reporting physical-unit effects.

```{r wind-data}
data("wind_newyork", package = "INLAcircular")
dim(wind_newyork)
utils::head(names(wind_newyork), 4)
```

This preparation uses January's records, centres direction about its sample
circular mean, standardizes the temperature covariate, and creates the hourly
node IDs expected by `x_model`:

```{r wind-prepare}
wind <- wind_newyork[wind_newyork$month == 1, ]
x <- as.numeric(wind$HLY.WIND.VCTDIR)
reference <- atan2(mean(sin(x)), mean(cos(x)))
x <- atan2(sin(x - reference), cos(x - reference))
wind_dat <- data.frame(
  x = x,
  z = as.numeric(scale(wind$HLY.TEMP.NORMAL)),
  hour = wind$hour + 1L
)
stopifnot(
  all(is.finite(as.matrix(wind_dat))),
  all(abs(wind_dat$x) < pi),
  all(wind_dat$hour %in% 1:24)
)
head(wind_dat, 3)
```

```{r wind-fit, eval=run_models}
wind_fit <- inlacc(
  x_model,
  data = wind_dat,
  latent.index = index(
    "hour_effect", data.id = wind_dat$hour, process.id = 1:24
  ),
  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE)
)
round(wind_fit$summary.fixed[, columns], 3)
round(wind_fit$summary.hyperpar[, columns], 3)
```

This is a small demonstration of the interface, not a complete analysis of
weather variability. The repository's `tests/manual/06-wind-new-york.R`
contains the larger joint circular-Gamma application. That developer script
requires INLA and `circular` and may take longer to run.

# Function index

| Area | Functions |
|:--|:--|
| Von Mises distribution | dvm, pvm, qvm, rvm |
| Link-adjusted von Mises | lavm.link, dlavm, plavm, qlavm, rlavm |
| Other circular densities | dcardioid (dcard), dwrappedcauchy (dwc) |
| Von Mises PC prior, uniform base | dpc.vm0, ppc.vm0, qpc.vm0, rpc.vm0 |
| Von Mises PC prior, point-mass base | dpc.vminf, ppc.vminf, qpc.vminf, rpc.vminf |
| Cardioid PC prior, uniform base | dpc.card0, ppc.card0, qpc.card0, rpc.card0 |
| Cardioid PC prior, kappa = 1/2 base | dpc.card, ppc.card, qpc.card, rpc.card |
| Wrapped Cauchy PC prior | dpc.wc, ppc.wc, qpc.wc, rpc.wc |
| Model specification | likelihood, intercept, covariate, index |
| Model fitting | inlacc, inla |
| Multivariate preprocessing | LKJcc |
| Results | summary.inlacc, print.inlacc_summary, print.inlacc_time |
| Numerical utility | bessel_i |
| Included data | wind_newyork |

Function-level help is available with `?function_name`. For names
containing dots, quote the topic if needed, for example
`help("dpc.card0")`.

# Numerical implementation notes

The cardioid and wrapped Cauchy routines use compiled C throughout their
numerical path. Endpoint limits, log-density calculations, inverse transforms,
and random generation are not implemented as R formulas. Cancellation-prone
expressions use algebraic reductions, `log1p()`,
`expm1()`, and local series near difficult boundaries.

# Troubleshooting and current limits

## Installation or function lookup

- If a fit reports that INLA is unavailable, install it from the stable
  repository shown above and check `packageVersion("INLA")`. Loading
  INLAcircular alone is enough for its fitting functions to find INLA.
- If `inla()` selects the wrong function after loading other packages, call
  `INLAcircular::inla()` explicitly. Keep `family = "lavm"` for this interface.
- If the installed vignette is missing after a GitHub installation, rebuild
  with `build_vignettes = TRUE` or read the repository HTML/PDF. Binary
  installations do not require the documentation tools to read a built guide.
- A compiler error during source installation concerns the R build
  environment. Check the platform-specific tools before trying model fits.
  Missing Pandoc or LaTeX affects documentation building, not the numerical API.

## Model specification and numerical behaviour

- Validate radians, the chosen reference direction, and the principal angle
  interval before fitting. Numerical clamping at a link boundary is not a
  replacement for wrapping circular data correctly.
- Supply LAvM concentration settings under `hyper$kappa`. Its `initial`
  value is `log(kappa)`. The `c(u, alpha)` prior calibration is distinct
  from the `lambda` argument of the standalone PC-prior functions.
- Ensure each latent index has one entry per data row and that its values
  belong to the specified `process.id` set. The wind data's raw hour field
  needs `+ 1L` when the latent nodes are `1:24`.
- Use numeric fixed-effect columns or explicitly prepared indicator columns.
  The model assembler does not implement every factor, offset, or special
  response-expression feature of R's `model.matrix()`.
- If a model has poorly identified effects, inspect duplicated predictors,
  copied terms, and prior sensitivity. Start with a simpler model, scale
  continuous covariates, and use `verbose = TRUE` to inspect INLA diagnostics.
- LKJ effects require `graphpcor` and `INLAtools`, at least two likelihood
  blocks, and matching index names. The exposed interface is a dense
  correlated IID effect; it is not the full graphpcor model catalogue.

INLA supplies approximate Bayesian inference. This guide demonstrates API
usage, not a guarantee of inferential accuracy for every data-generating
process. Check modelling assumptions and sensitivity for the application.
The distribution p/q/r functions currently use the inverse-tangent LAvM
transformation, even though fitting supports additional links. The fitted
positive concentration prior has the boundary limitation described in the
LAvM controls section, and LAvM PIT is currently unavailable.

## Reproducible computation and support

Numerical summaries and run times may differ with R, INLA, dependency
versions, platform, and thread settings. Preserve seeds, input preparation,
priors, and the environment information at the end of this guide.

Report reproducible problems at the
[issue tracker](https://github.com/XiangYEstats/INLAcircular/issues).
Include a small data example or simulation, the complete model call, the
error text, and `sessionInfo()`. For maintainer contact, use
`maintainer("INLAcircular")`. Do not include private data in a public issue.

# Rebuilding and testing

## Repository layout

The repository follows the standard R package structure:

| Location | Purpose |
|:--|:--|
| `R/` | Public R functions and model assembly |
| `src/` | Compiled numerical routines and fitting integration |
| `man/` | Generated function help and CRAN reference-manual source |
| `vignettes/` | This guide's executable R Markdown source |
| `tools/render-guide.R` | Rebuild the repository HTML and PDF guides |
| `tests/` | Automated numerical and interface regression tests |
| `tests/manual/` | Longer developer models and application checks |
| `data/`, `inst/` | Packaged data, citations, and licensing notices |
| `output/html/`, `output/pdf/` | Rendered repository documentation |

The numerical layer is callable without INLA. The modelling layer translates
`likelihood()`, formula terms, and index mappings into an INLA model;
`inlacc()` returns the INLA result with package-specific summaries and
metadata. LKJ preprocessing is delegated to `graphpcor` when requested.

## Rebuild the guide

From a clone or downloaded source tree, install the documentation packages:

```{r documentation-dependencies, eval=FALSE}
install.packages(c("knitr", "rmarkdown", "pkgload"))
```

Install Pandoc and a LaTeX distribution containing `pdflatex` for both formats.
Then run one of these commands from the repository root:

```sh
Rscript tools/render-guide.R
Rscript tools/render-guide.R --run-models
Rscript tools/render-guide.R --run-lkj
```

The first command builds the lightweight edition. The second also executes
the ordinary INLA examples, including the small wind fit. The third includes
the LKJ examples and requires all optional modelling dependencies. These
commands use the current source package, fail on missing requested
dependencies, and overwrite the two rendered guide files. Model execution
occurs separately for HTML and PDF. The output records which examples ran;
successful completion means all enabled chunks evaluated without error.

The RStudio Knit button and VS Code knitting shortcut use the same YAML
render function. To build only the installable HTML vignette through the
standard package workflow, use `R CMD build` as described next; that path
does not require LaTeX for this HTML vignette.

## Check the package

Install the declared dependencies before running a package check. INLA is
installed from its separate repository; `graphpcor`, `INLAtools`, and the
documentation packages are optional dependencies for the complete checks.
In a terminal at the repository root:

```sh
R CMD build .
R CMD check --as-cran INLAcircular_1.0.0.tar.gz
```

Use the archive name printed by `R CMD build` if the package version differs.
The standard check runs function examples, automated tests, and vignette
checks. PDF reference-manual checking also requires LaTeX. To run a specific
longer developer example after installing this source version:

```sh
R CMD INSTALL .
Rscript tests/manual/01-direct-inla-lavm.R
Rscript tests/manual/02-joint-circular-linear.R
```

See `tests/manual/README.md` in the repository for the remaining scripts and
their dependency requirements. These longer applications are deliberately
outside the automatic CRAN test path. The CI configuration declares checks
for Linux, Windows, and macOS, plus a minimum-R core-dependency job. Consult
the actual run logs before claiming that a particular version passed on all
platforms.

Automated tests cover numerical boundaries, missing values, probability and
quantile consistency, optional-INLA behaviour, LAvM controls, copied
predictors, and LKJ preprocessing. Passing these checks demonstrates those
tested behaviours; it is not a benchmark or proof of model accuracy for
every application.

## Identify the version used in a publication

Repository links under `main` change over time. For a paper or archived
analysis, record the release tag or full commit SHA, the package version,
the dependency versions, and the guide built from that same source. A local
Git checkout can report its commit with:

```sh
git rev-parse HEAD
```

Use the corresponding commit or release URL for the source and guide links
in the article's software metadata. Record any local modifications as well;
the version in `DESCRIPTION` alone does not identify an uncommitted source
tree. A versioned archive DOI, when one has been created, can supplement the
repository link. This guide does not assert that an archive or release tag
already exists.

# Citation and license

Use the package's citation information for the circular-regression framework
and the PC-prior methods:

```{r citation-instructions, eval=FALSE}
citation("INLAcircular")
toBibtex(citation("INLAcircular"))
```

The method references are Ye, Van Niekerk, and Rue's
[circular regression framework](https://doi.org/10.1093/jrsssc/qlag056)
in *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series C: Applied Statistics*
and [PC priors for circular models](https://doi.org/10.1177/1471082X261453677)
in *Statistical Modelling*.
The installed `CITATION` file is the maintained source for their bibliographic
entries. Cite the software version used as well as the applicable methods.

INLAcircular is distributed under GNU GPL version 3 or later, as recorded in
`DESCRIPTION`. The full license and third-party notices are available through
the repository and in an installed package:

```{r license-locations}
basename(system.file("LICENSES", "GPL-3", package = "INLAcircular"))
basename(system.file("COPYRIGHTS", package = "INLAcircular"))
```

# Build environment

These values describe the environment that rendered this edition, not a
claim that the listed versions are the only supported versions. An optional
package being installed does not mean its examples were executed; see the
evaluation statement in Quick start.

```{r package-versions}
packages <- c("INLAcircular", "INLA", "graphpcor", "INLAtools")
versions <- vapply(packages, function(package) {
  if (requireNamespace(package, quietly = TRUE)) {
    as.character(packageVersion(package))
  } else {
    "not installed"
  }
}, character(1))
data.frame(package = packages, version = unname(versions))
```

```{r session-info}
sessionInfo()
```
